passage: For the Class 10 farewell at the government school in the kasba, Saurabh listed every cost on the back of a notebook page: samosas, tea, a banner, decorations. Total: 2,400 rupees. With thirty classmates that came to eighty each, but Rashmi, who kept the class money box, said, "Some can't give eighty. Make it fifty." So Saurabh went back to the list. Shop samosas cost nine hundred, but if mothers made pakoras at home, three hundred. The art club could paint the banner. Rashmi drew a big sheet on chart paper and pinned it to the classroom wall: every name, every payment, every purchase. By Friday it showed 1,420 collected and 1,180 spent. "Left: 240," Rashmi wrote, "for the tea."

qa.q: How much was each classmate asked to give in the end?
qa.a: Each classmate was asked to give fifty.

qa.q: Why did Rashmi want the limit lowered, and how did Saurabh respond?
qa.a: Rashmi worried that some classmates could not afford eighty, and Saurabh accepted it and went back to the list to find cheaper options.

qa.q: What else could Saurabh do if collections run short, and why?
qa.a: Saurabh could cut the decorations or ask a shopkeeper for a small donation of tea leaves, because the shared sheet shows exactly where money can be saved.

qa.q: How might a classmate who cannot afford much see the fifty rupee limit?
qa.a: That classmate would likely feel relieved and included, since the party stays affordable and everything is written openly on the wall.

grounding: The organiser lists all expected costs, sets what each classmate can contribute, prices alternatives such as home-made snacks, and tracks spending on a shared sheet.

passage: Emeka's class in Lagos wanted an end-of-term party, and Emeka had volunteered to organise it with Leila. First he listed every cost he could think of: drinks, snacks, decorations, a speaker, paper plates. Then he asked the class, anonymously on slips of paper, what each person could comfortably give. Some wrote very little. So they set one small contribution everyone could manage, and agreed that nobody had to explain giving less. With that total, hiring a speaker was out; Leila's cousin would lend one. Bought snacks cost too much, so Leila priced home-made puff-puff and chin chin against shop packets. Home-made won easily, and four parents offered to help fry. Every naira spent went into a shared sheet the whole class could see. At the party there was even a little left over for next term.

qa.q: Why did Emeka ask about contributions anonymously?
qa.a: He was worried that some classmates would feel embarrassed saying how little they could give in front of others.

qa.q: What makes the shared sheet useful?
qa.a: Everyone can see where the money goes, which builds trust and keeps spending within the agreed total.

qa.q: How might classmates who could give only a little feel about the plan?
qa.a: They are likely relieved and included, since the amount was set for everyone and no one had to explain giving less.

grounding: Shows an organiser listing costs, setting a contribution everyone can manage, pricing home-made snacks and tracking spending in a shared sheet.

passage: In the Class 11 common room, Rehana pinned a chart to the noticeboard: "Farewell for Class 12: costs." Hall decoration, a cake, snacks, a sound system, printed cards. Jagdish Sir, the staff advisor, looked it over. "And how much are you asking each student for?" "Nobody pays more than what we agreed in class, the smallest amount anyone suggested," Rehana said. "So I've been pricing cheaper options." The sound system: the school's own, free if the office staff help set it up. Printed cards: handmade in art period. Snacks: she had compared a caterer with parents making samosas and sandwiches, and home-made cost less than half. "Every rupee goes in this sheet," she said, tapping a shared file on the class tablet. "Anyone can check." Jagdish Sir nodded slowly. "You've done this better than the teachers did last year."

qa.q: What will replace the printed cards?
How might Rehana feel when Jagdish Sir praises the plan?
qa.a: She probably feels proud and pleased that her careful planning was noticed.

qa.q: Why is setting the contribution at the smallest agreed amount a fair choice?
qa.a: It lets every student take part without strain, and pushes the planning toward cheaper options instead of asking for more.

qa.q: How does Jagdish Sir see Rehana's chart?
qa.a: He is impressed, saying she has done it better than the teachers did last year.

grounding: Shows an organiser listing expected costs, capping each classmate's contribution, pricing cheaper alternatives and tracking spending in a shared sheet.
